title: Migration & Globalisation
description: Why people move, the difference between migrants and refugees, and how trade, technology and TNCs have stitched the world into one connected system — with winners and losers.

notes.heading: 📌 What is Migration? Types of Movement
notes.body: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another with the intention of settling, temporarily or permanently. Geographers classify it in two main ways. By distance and borders: internal migration happens within a country (for example, rural-urban migration from the countryside to a city, or moving between regions for work); international migration crosses national borders. By choice: voluntary migration is a free decision made to improve life — for work, family, education or lifestyle; forced migration happens when people have no safe choice but to leave, fleeing war, persecution, natural disasters or human trafficking. Emigration means leaving a country (emigrants leave); immigration means arriving in one (immigrants arrive) — the same person is both. Net migration is the difference between the two: positive when more people arrive than leave, negative when more leave than arrive. Most migration in the world today is internal, and most international migration is between neighbouring countries.

notes.heading: 🔑 Push and Pull Factors
notes.body: Every migration decision can be analysed as a balance of push factors (negative conditions that drive people away from a place) and pull factors (positive attractions that draw people to a new place). Common push factors: unemployment and low wages, poverty, war and persecution, food shortages and drought, poor healthcare and education, natural hazards, and political instability. Common pull factors: job opportunities and higher wages, better schools and hospitals, safety and political freedom, family already living there (chain migration), and a higher overall quality of life. Between the pushes and pulls sit intervening obstacles — things that make moving hard: distance and cost, visas and border controls, language barriers, and dangerous journeys. Migration is rarely about one factor alone; a young worker might be pushed by unemployment, pulled by wages, and stopped by the cost of a visa. The same factor can be a push or a pull depending on perspective — low wages push people out of one country and pull employers into it.

notes.heading: 📎 Refugees and Asylum Seekers
notes.body: A refugee is someone forced to flee their country because of war, violence or persecution based on their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a social group — and who cannot safely return. An asylum seeker is a person who has arrived in another country and asked for protection but whose claim has not yet been decided; if the claim is accepted, they gain refugee status. An internally displaced person (IDP) has fled for the same reasons but remains inside their own country — and there are far more IDPs in the world than refugees. Journeys are often dangerous and desperate: crowded boats, long walks through hostile territory, paying smugglers, and months or years in refugee camps such as those in Jordan, Kenya or Bangladesh. Most refugees — around three-quarters — are hosted not by rich countries but by neighbouring low- and middle-income countries. Host countries face real pressures on housing, schools and health services, but refugees also bring skills, fill labour shortages and start businesses once they can work. Economic migrants, by contrast, move primarily for work and a better life rather than to escape danger.

notes.heading: 🔑 Impacts of Migration and Diasporas
notes.body: Migration transforms both the places people leave and the places they arrive in. Impacts on the country of origin: positive — remittances (money migrants send home) are a huge income source, exceeding global aid; returning migrants bring new skills and ideas; pressure on jobs and housing eases. Negative — the loss of young, educated workers (the brain drain), ageing populations left behind, and families split apart. Impacts on the host country: positive — migrants fill labour shortages (in health care, construction, agriculture), pay taxes, start businesses and enrich culture with food, music and ideas; negative or challenging — short-term pressure on housing, schools and hospitals, and tensions if integration is poorly managed. Over time, migrant communities form diasporas — networks of people from one origin living abroad who keep ties to their homeland. The Chinese, Indian, Irish and Nigerian diasporas each number in the tens of millions. Diasporas send remittances, trade links, skills and culture in both directions, and keep languages and traditions alive far from home.

notes.heading: 📌 What is Globalisation?
notes.body: Globalisation is the process by which the world's countries, economies, cultures and people have become increasingly interconnected and interdependent — as if the world is shrinking. It is driven by several forces working together. Trade: goods, services and money flow across borders more freely than ever, helped by trade agreements and container shipping, which slashed transport costs. Technology: the internet, smartphones, satellites and cheap flights allow information, money and people to move almost instantly — a video call between continents is now free. Transnational corporations (TNCs): huge companies such as Apple, Nike, Toyota and McDonald's operate in dozens of countries, designing products in one place, manufacturing in another and selling everywhere. Culture: films, music, food, fashion and sport spread globally, creating a shared global culture — the same brands and songs appear on every continent. Flows of people (migration and tourism) and flows of capital (investment) complete the web. Globalisation is not entirely new — trade routes like the Silk Road are ancient — but its speed and scale since the late twentieth century are unprecedented.

notes.heading: 🔑 How Globalisation Works: TNCs and the Global Supply Chain
notes.body: A smartphone illustrates the global supply chain: designed in the USA, using rare metals mined in Africa, chips made in Taiwan or South Korea, assembled in China or Vietnam, shipped by container vessel and sold worldwide. TNCs organise production this way to cut costs — seeking cheap labour, low taxes, weak regulation or proximity to raw materials and markets. This brings benefits to host countries: jobs, investment, technology transfer and tax revenue, which helped countries like China industrialise at record speed. But there are drawbacks: wages and working conditions in factories can be poor; profits often flow back to headquarters in rich countries; TNCs can relocate suddenly, devastating a town built around one factory; and environmental standards may be weaker where production moves. Containerisation — standardised steel boxes loaded straight from factory to ship to lorry — cut shipping costs dramatically and is one of the quiet revolutions behind globalisation. Communication technology lets a company coordinate this whole chain in real time. Global supply chains are efficient but fragile: the COVID-19 pandemic and blocked shipping lanes showed how a disruption in one place empties shelves everywhere.

notes.heading: 💡 Winners and Losers of Globalisation
notes.body: Globalisation has lifted hundreds of millions out of extreme poverty, but its benefits are unevenly shared. Winners: consumers in rich countries enjoy cheap goods and huge choice; workers in industrialising countries such as China, Vietnam and Bangladesh gained factory jobs and rising incomes; skilled workers and big companies can operate globally; global cooperation has improved responses to disease and disasters. Losers: factory workers in rich countries lost jobs when production moved overseas; the poorest countries that supply only raw materials are stuck at the bottom of the value chain; workers in sweatshops face low pay and unsafe conditions; local cultures and languages can be swamped by global brands; and the environment pays through pollution, shipping emissions and deforestation. Food and health reveal the inequality starkly. Food: global trade means some regions feast on imported produce all year while others face famine — famines today are rarely about an absolute shortage of food globally, but about poverty, war and failed distribution, as in conflicts that block food aid. Health: wealthy countries enjoy advanced medicine and high life expectancy while diseases like malaria kill hundreds of thousands of children yearly in poor countries, and during COVID-19 vaccines reached rich countries years before the poorest. Globalisation connects us — but the connections are not yet fair.

flashcards.definition: The movement of people from one place to another with the intention of settling, temporarily or permanently.
flashcards.example: A nurse moving from the Philippines to work in the UK is an example of international migration.

flashcards.definition: Migration within a country's own borders — for example, from rural areas to cities or between regions.
flashcards.example: A family moving from a village in northern China to Shanghai for work is internal migration.

flashcards.definition: A negative condition that drives people to leave a place, such as war, unemployment, poverty or drought.
flashcards.example: A failed harvest and food shortages push farming families to leave their village.

flashcards.definition: A positive attraction that draws people to a new place, such as jobs, higher wages, safety or better schools.
flashcards.example: Well-paid hospital jobs and political stability pull skilled workers towards countries like Canada.

flashcards.definition: A person forced to flee their country because of war, violence or persecution, who cannot safely return home.
flashcards.example: Millions of Syrians became refugees in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan during the civil war.

flashcards.definition: Someone who has asked another country for protection as a refugee but whose claim has not yet been decided.
flashcards.example: An asylum seeker who is granted protection receives refugee status and the right to stay.

flashcards.definition: A person forced to flee home by war or disaster who remains inside their own country's borders.
flashcards.example: People sheltering in camps after fleeing fighting within their own country are IDPs, not refugees.

flashcards.definition: Money that migrants working abroad send back to their families in their home country.
flashcards.example: Remittances to countries like India and the Philippines are larger than all foreign aid they receive.

flashcards.definition: The loss of highly educated and skilled workers from a country through emigration.
flashcards.example: When many doctors trained in a poor country leave to work abroad, its health service suffers a brain drain.

flashcards.definition: A network of people from the same origin living in many countries abroad, keeping ties to their homeland.
flashcards.example: The Indian diaspora — millions of people of Indian origin worldwide — sustains trade, remittances and cultural links.

flashcards.definition: The growing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures and populations through trade, technology, transport and migration.
flashcards.example: Buying clothes designed in Europe, made in Bangladesh and advertised on a US-owned app is globalisation in action.

flashcards.definition: A large company that operates in many countries, often designing, producing and selling in different parts of the world.
flashcards.example: Nike designs shoes in the USA, manufactures them in Asia and sells them in shops worldwide.

choices: The movement of goods between countries
The movement of people from one place to another to settle, temporarily or permanently
The growth of cities
The spread of technology around the world
questions.explanation: Migration means people moving to live somewhere new, whether within a country or across borders. Trade in goods or the spread of technology are parts of globalisation, not migration.

questions.stem: A person moves from a small village to the capital city of their own country. What type of migration is this?
choices: International migration
Forced migration
Internal (rural-urban) migration
Seasonal migration
questions.explanation: The move never crosses a national border, so it is internal migration — specifically rural-urban migration, the most common type worldwide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pull factor?
choices: War and persecution in the home country
Higher wages and job opportunities in the destination country
Drought destroying crops at home
Overcrowded housing at home
questions.explanation: Pull factors are attractions of the destination — jobs, wages, safety and services. War, drought and overcrowding are push factors that drive people away from the origin.

choices: Anyone who moves country for a better-paid job
A person forced to flee their country because of war, violence or persecution, who cannot safely return
A person who moves within their own country for work
A tourist who stays abroad too long
questions.explanation: Refugees are defined by being forced to flee danger and persecution and being unable to return safely. Moving for better pay makes someone an economic migrant, not a refugee.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a refugee and an asylum seeker?
choices: There is no difference — the words mean the same thing
An asylum seeker has applied for protection but their claim is not yet decided; a refugee's claim has been accepted
Refugees travel by boat while asylum seekers travel by plane
Asylum seekers always have their claims rejected
questions.explanation: An asylum seeker is waiting for a decision on their request for protection. Only if the claim is accepted do they gain refugee status and the legal right to stay.

questions.stem: Which statement about where refugees live is correct?
choices: Most refugees are hosted by wealthy countries in Europe and North America
Around three-quarters of refugees are hosted by neighbouring low- and middle-income countries
All refugees live permanently in camps
Refugees are evenly shared between every country in the world
questions.explanation: Contrary to media impressions, most refugees stay close to home: countries like Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, Uganda and Bangladesh host far more refugees than rich Western nations, putting heavy strain on those hosts' services.

choices: Taxes that migrants pay to the host government
Money that migrants working abroad send back to family in their home country
Payments companies make to build factories overseas
Aid given by charities to refugees
questions.explanation: Remittances are migrants' earnings sent home — globally worth more than all foreign aid combined, making them a vital income source for many poorer countries.

questions.stem: A country loses many of its newly trained doctors and engineers to better-paid jobs abroad. What is this called?
choices: Chain migration
Urbanisation
Brain drain
Counter-urbanisation
questions.explanation: The brain drain is the loss of educated, skilled workers through emigration — a serious cost to origin countries that paid for their training but lose their skills and taxes.

choices: A refugee camp near a border
A network of people from the same origin living across many countries who keep ties to their homeland
A type of trade agreement
The border zone between two countries
questions.explanation: A diaspora is a scattered community — like the Chinese, Indian or Irish diasporas — whose members live abroad but sustain cultural, family and economic links with their homeland.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best definition of globalisation?
choices: The growth of the world's population
The process by which countries, economies, cultures and people become increasingly interconnected and interdependent
The building of taller buildings in world cities
The spread of democracy to every country
questions.explanation: Globalisation is about connection — trade, technology, transport, migration and culture linking the world so that events and decisions in one place affect people everywhere.

questions.stem: A company designs trainers in the USA, manufactures them in Vietnam and sells them in shops across Europe. What kind of organisation is this?
choices: A charity
A nationalised industry
A local business
A transnational corporation (TNC)
questions.explanation: Operating across many countries — splitting design, production and sales between them to cut costs and reach markets — is the defining feature of a transnational corporation.

questions.stem: How did containerisation help drive globalisation?
choices: Standardised steel containers made shipping goods around the world far cheaper and faster
It allowed people to travel between countries without passports
It meant all products had to be made in the same country
It replaced ships with aeroplanes for all cargo
questions.explanation: Standard containers transfer directly from factory to ship to lorry, slashing loading times and transport costs. Cheaper shipping made it profitable to manufacture on the other side of the world — a quiet engine of global trade.

questions.stem: Which group has generally been a 'loser' from globalisation in high-income countries?
choices: Consumers who can buy cheaper imported goods
Factory workers whose jobs moved overseas to lower-wage countries
Shareholders in large TNCs
Skilled workers able to work anywhere in the world
questions.explanation: When TNCs relocate production to countries with cheaper labour, manufacturing towns in rich countries lose jobs and industries. Consumers and companies gain, but displaced workers bear the cost.

questions.stem: Geographers argue that modern famines are rarely caused by a global shortage of food. What is the main reason they happen?
choices: The world genuinely cannot grow enough food for its population
Poverty, war and failed distribution stop food reaching the people who need it
People in famine regions refuse to eat imported food
Farming technology has stopped improving
questions.explanation: The world produces enough food for everyone; famines occur when conflict blocks supply routes, when people are too poor to buy food, or when governments fail to distribute it — an inequality problem, not a production problem.

questions.stem: A TNC suddenly closes its factory and moves production to another country with lower wages. Which combination of impacts is most likely?
choices: The abandoned town loses jobs while profits continue flowing to the TNC's headquarters country
The abandoned town immediately becomes richer
Wages in the town rise because the factory has left
The TNC must keep paying all its former workers forever
questions.explanation: TNCs can relocate quickly, and towns dependent on a single employer are hit hard — job losses, falling local spending and empty buildings — while the company's profits still flow back to its home country. This is a core criticism of globalisation's unevenness.
